name: John Climacus
knownFor: Monk and abbot of Mount Sinai who wrote the Ladder, a guide to the monk's life in thirty steps, at the request of John, abbot of Raithu. Philippe Labbe says he was called Climacus after the book.
dates: No source used here gives his years. The Library file's header gives about 579 to 649, which is a header and not a source. Philippe Labbe says he lived about 580, and argues that if a Sinai monk's tale is true he died between 560 and 565. The Bollandists find a death about 580, or at least near the end of the sixth century, likely. James Barmby reports that he is said to have died early in the seventh century. Labbe and the Bollandists say the Greeks keep his day on 30 March
place: Mount Sinai. Daniel of Raithu says he came there at sixteen, lived alone at Tholas, five miles from the church, and was made head of the monastery. Daniel cannot say where he was born
role: Monk, hermit and abbot of the monastery on Mount Sinai; writer of the Ladder

keyWorks.title: The Ladder (Scala Paradisi)
keyWorks.about: thirty steps of the monk's life, from leaving the world to faith, hope and love, written at the request of John, abbot of Raithu. At its end John ties the thirty steps to Christ's age at his baptism

keyWorks.title: Book to the Shepherd (Liber ad Pastorem)
keyWorks.about: a short book on the work of an abbot, which likens him to a shepherd, a ship's master, a doctor and a teacher

traces: Philippe Labbe says the Greeks held him in great value, as the Questions of Athanasius, Elias of Crete, Theodore the Studite, Philip the Solitary and John Zonaras show. Elias of Crete, he says, wrote explanations of the Ladder.
Labbe reports that the Ladder is said to have been first put into Latin in 1295 by Angelo Clareno, and that it was printed at Venice in 1590 in the everyday Greek of the time.
Matthew Rader's Greek and Latin edition of his works, with the Life by Daniel of Raithu and the Greek notes on the Ladder, is the text Migne reprints.
remembered: Thomas à Kempis, of John Ketel, a cook in the House of Florentius: "Sometimes he read the book of John Climacus “On perfect renunciation of the world and mortification of the Will,” and expounded therefrom sentiments full of spiritual truth." Thomas says wise men marveled at how well he understood the book.
Cardinal Baronius, as Rader and the Bollandists report him, says a divine likeness of his soul is seen far more clearly in his writings.
Jean Gerson found things in the Ladder to fault. Rader answers that nothing in the whole of Climacus is false or against the church's decrees, though much is misunderstood.

uncertain: His life comes mainly from the short Life by Daniel, a monk of Raithu. The Bollandists say Daniel wrote it soon after John's death, while John, abbot of Raithu, still lived. It is a saint's Life, with a vision and a cure by prayer. Daniel says he cannot tell for sure where John was born or how he was raised. More tales come from an unnamed monk of Sinai, of John's own time, whom Matthew Rader and the Bollandists print after the Life.

His years. The Library header's 579 to 649 rests on no held line. Philippe Labbe places him about 580. He reports the reckoning of Antonius Magister, a French translator of the Ladder: born about 525, a monk at sixteen, dead in 605 or 606. Labbe says the sums do not add up. He then argues from the years of Peter, patriarch of Jerusalem, in Theophanes, Evagrius and Nicephorus that if the Sinai monk's tale is true John died between 560 and 565. He concludes that hardly anything certain can be said of the year of his death, of his entry into the monastery, of his time in the desert or of when he became abbot. The Bollandists judge Labbe's 580 likely, or at least the end of the sixth century. James Barmby reports that he is said to have been elected abbot at seventy-five and to have died early in the seventh century.

Pope Gregory the Great's letter to John, abbot of Mount Sinai. Gregory sent cloaks, blankets and beds for a house for the aged built there by one Isaurus, in Barmby's English. Paul Ewald and Ludwig Hartmann date the letter 1 September 600 and point to Rader's edition for Climacus's life. Barmby says the John addressed is "No doubt" Climacus. Labbe's reckoning would put John's death at least thirty-five years before the letter.

His early years on Sinai. Rader's Latin of Daniel has him take up the life alone as he began his twentieth year. The short summary of the Life that Rader prints, and the Menologium of the emperor Basil as the Bollandists give it, say he went to Tholas nineteen years after he came to Sinai. The Sinai monk says Abbot Martyrius made him a monk at twenty; Rader takes Daniel's sixteen as his entry as a novice.
His age at death. Labbe says the Greek Menaea make him nearly a hundred when he died, if they are to be trusted.

His brother George. In the Sinai monk's tale, John told George he would not finish the year without following him. Rader's Latin and Greek say George died within ten months; the Bollandists' Latin reads ten years. John Moschus tells of a George, abbot on Sinai, who wrote to Peter, patriarch of Jerusalem, that they would both die in six months. Labbe links Moschus's account to the tale. Rader doubts that Moschus's George was John's brother.
The time of his life. Johannes Trithemius placed him under the sons of Constantine. Rader, Labbe and the Bollandists reject this, since John wrote after Sabas, who died in 532.

Namesakes. He is a different man from John, abbot of Raithu, who asked for the Ladder; from John Moschus; from John the Faster, patriarch of Constantinople, whose Penitential stands in the same Migne volume; and from John the Sabaite, who in the Sinai monk's tale washed his feet. Labbe reports another John, abbot of Sinai, whom manuscripts name as author of the story of Barlaam and Josaphat. Rader holds that Climacus did not write it.
